title: Definition
body_md:
Let $M$ be a real-analytic hypersurface invariant by $\mathcal F$ and satisfying
$\operatorname{Sing}(M)\subset\operatorname{Sing}(\mathcal F)$. Let
\(
p\in M\cap\operatorname{Sing}(\mathcal F)
\)
be a dicritical singularity, and let
\(
F_p=\frac{f}{g}:U_p\dashrightarrow\mathbb P^1
\)
be a minimal local meromorphic first integral of the germ $(\mathcal F,p)$.
We say that $p$ is a \emph{pencil singularity for $M$} if:
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)}]
\item
\[
p\in\overline L
\]
for every Levi leaf $L\subset M_{\mathrm{reg}}$;
\item for every generic global Levi leaf $L\subset M_{\mathrm{reg}}$, the
restriction of $F_p$ to $L\cap U_p$ is constant (where the
restriction is understood off the indeterminacy set of $F_p$).
\end{enumerate}
Equivalently, for every generic global Levi leaf $L$ there exists a
unique $\lambda(L)\in\mathbb P^1$ such that every local component of
$L\cap U_p$ sufficiently near $p$ is contained in
\[
V_{\lambda(L)}=\{f-\lambda(L)g=0\}.
\]
This property is independent of the chosen minimal first integral,
since two minimal generators differ by a M\"obius transformation.
head: environment
name: Pencil singularity

label: thm:plane-characterization
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:plane-characterization}
Let $\mathcal F$ be a holomorphic foliation on $\mathbb P^2$. The following
conditions are equivalent.

\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)}]
\item $\mathcal F$ admits a primitive nonconstant rational first integral
\[
R:\mathbb P^2\dashrightarrow\mathbb P^1.
\]

\item There exists an irreducible real-analytic variety of pure real codimension one 
\(
M\subset\mathbb P^2
\)
invariant by $\mathcal F$, with
\(
\operatorname{Sing}(M)\subset\operatorname{Sing}(\mathcal F),
\)
and all the dicritical singularities
\(
p_1,\ldots,p_r\in M\cap\operatorname{Sing}(\mathcal F)
\)
of $\mathcal F$ on $M$, together with local meromorphic first integrals
\[
H_j:(U_j,p_j)\dashrightarrow\mathbb P^1,
\qquad j=1,\ldots,r,
\]
such that every Levi leaf $L\subset M_{\mathrm{reg}}$ accumulates at least
one of the points $p_j$, and:
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\alph*)}]
\item for every generic global Levi leaf $L\subset M_{\mathrm{reg}}$ approaching
$p_j$, the restriction $H_j|_{L\cap U_j}$ is constant; denote its value
by $\lambda_j(L)$;
\item there exist transformations
\[
A_{ji}\in\operatorname{PGL}(2,\mathbb C)
\]
satisfying
\[
A_{ii}=\operatorname{id},
\qquad
A_{kj}\circ A_{ji}=A_{ki}
\]
whenever the corresponding continuations are defined;
\item whenever a generic global Levi leaf $L$ accumulates at both
$p_i$ and $p_j$, one has
\[
\lambda_j(L)=A_{ji}\bigl(\lambda_i(L)\bigr).
\]
\end{enumerate}
\end{enumerate}
head: environment
name: Characterization in the projective plane

label: cor:single-dicritical-plane
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{cor:single-dicritical-plane}
Let $\mathcal F$ be a codimension-one holomorphic foliation on $\mathbb P^2$
preserving an irreducible real-analytic variety of pure real codimension one  $M$. Assume
\[
\operatorname{Sing}(M)\subset\operatorname{Sing}(\mathcal F).
\]
Suppose that $p\in M\cap\operatorname{Sing}(\mathcal F)$ is the only dicritical
singularity of $\mathcal F$ on $M$ and that $p$ is a pencil singularity for $M$.
Then $\mathcal F$ admits a nonconstant rational first integral on $\mathbb P^2$.
head: environment
name: A single dicritical singularity

label: thm:projective-main
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:projective-main}
Let $\mathcal F$ be a codimension-one holomorphic foliation on $\mathbb P^n$,
$n\ge3$, and let $M\subset\mathbb P^n$ be an irreducible real-analytic variety of pure real codimension one invariant by $\mathcal F$. Assume:

\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)}]
\item
\(
\operatorname{Sing}(M)\subset\operatorname{Sing}(\mathcal F);
\)

\item all dicritical singularities of $\mathcal F$ contained in $M$ belong to
an irreducible codimension-two analytic subset
\(
D\subset M\cap\operatorname{Sing}(\mathcal F),
\)
and $D$ is generically of local product type;

\item there exists a pencil singularity for $M$ in the local-product
locus of $D$;
\end{enumerate}

Then $\mathcal F$ admits a nonconstant rational first integral
\[
R:\mathbb P^n\dashrightarrow\mathbb P^1.
\]
head: environment
name: Projective integrability criterion

label: cor:local-separation
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{cor:local-separation}
Let $\mathcal F$ be a codimension-one holomorphic foliation on $\mathbb P^n$,
$n\ge3$, and let $M\subset\mathbb P^n$ be an irreducible real-analytic variety of pure real codimension one invariant by $\mathcal F$. Assume that
\[
\operatorname{Sing}(M)\subset\operatorname{Sing}(\mathcal F),
\]
that all dicritical singularities of $\mathcal F$ contained in $M$ belong to
an irreducible codimension-two analytic subset
\[
D\subset M\cap\operatorname{Sing}(\mathcal F)
\]
which is generically of local product type. Assume that each Levi leaf
$L\subset M_{\mathrm{reg}}$ accumulates at some point in the local-product
locus of $D$. Fix a point $p$ in this locus and let
\[
F_p:U_p\dashrightarrow\mathbb P^1
\]
be a minimal local meromorphic first integral of the germ $(\mathcal F,p)$.
Suppose that, after shrinking $U_p$, there exist a real-analytic
one-dimensional manifold $S$ and a real-analytic map
\[
h:M_{\mathrm{reg}}\cap U_p\longrightarrow S
\]
which separates the nearby Levi leaves at $p$ and has the following
global-leaf compatibility property: for every generic global Levi leaf
$L\subset M_{\mathrm{reg}}$, the restriction $h|_{L\cap U_p}$ is constant.
Then $p$ is a pencil singularity for $M$, and consequently $\mathcal F$ admits a
nonconstant rational first integral on $\mathbb P^n$.
head: environment
name: Local transverse separation criterion

label: thm:leviflat-intersection-alternative
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:leviflat-intersection-alternative}
Let $\mathcal F$ be a holomorphic foliation on $\mathbb P^2$ and let
$\{M_\alpha\}_{\alpha\in A}$ be infinitely many pairwise distinct
irreducible invariant real-analytic Levi-flat varieties. Assume that
there is one member $M_0$ for which
\(
(M_0\cap M_\alpha)\setminus\operatorname{Sing}(\mathcal F)\ne\varnothing
\)
for infinitely many $\alpha$. Assume moreover that
\(
\operatorname{Sing}(M_\alpha)\subset\operatorname{Sing}(\mathcal F)
\)
for every $\alpha\in A$. Then either $\mathcal F$ admits a nonconstant
rational first integral, or there is an irreducible invariant algebraic
curve $C$ contained in infinitely many $M_\alpha$. In the second
alternative the virtual holonomy group of every connected regular leaf
component of $C\setminus\operatorname{Sing}(\mathcal F)$ is abelian.
head: environment
name: Infinite-family alternative

label: corollary:abelian
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{corollary:abelian}
Under (ii) in Theorem~\ref{thm:leviflat-intersection-alternative}, assume, in addition, that the singularities of $\mathcal F$ on $C$ satisfy the following conditions:
\begin{enumerate}
\item every non-dicritical singularity of $\mathcal F$ on $C$ is reduced and nondegenerate, i.e., it is of the form
\[
x\,dy-\lambda y\,dx+(\cdots)=0,
\qquad \lambda\in\mathbb C^*\setminus\mathbb Q_{>0};
\]
\item the dicritical singularities are $p_1,\ldots,p_m\in C\cap\operatorname{Sing}(\mathcal F)$ and, after one blow-up at each $p_j$, every singularity of the transformed foliation lying on the strict transform of $C$ is reduced, non-dicritical, and is not a saddle-node.
\end{enumerate}
 Put
\[
d_j=\operatorname{mult}_{p_j}(C).
\]
If
\[
\sum_{j=1}^m d_j<\deg C,
\]
then $\mathcal F$ is defined on $\mathbb P^2$ by a nonzero closed rational $1$-form.
If, in addition, the reduction of singularities of $\mathcal F$ contains no
saddle-nodes, then $\mathcal F$ is defined by a closed logarithmic rational
$1$-form.
head: environment

label: ex:pencil
title: Example
body_md:
\label{ex:pencil}
Let
\[
R=\frac{F}{G}:\mathbb P^n\dashrightarrow\mathbb P^1,
\]
where $F$ and $G$ are homogeneous polynomials of the same degree, and
suppose that $R$ is a rational first integral of a codimension-one
foliation $\mathcal F$.  Let $\gamma\subset\mathbb P^1$ be a real-analytic curve and
set
\[
M=\overline{R^{-1}(\gamma)}.
\]
Away from the critical and indeterminacy loci of $R$, use local
coordinates
\[
(z_1,\ldots,z_{n-1},t),\qquad t=R.
\]
If $\rho(t,\overline t)=0$ is a real-analytic equation for $\gamma$,
then $M$ is locally defined by the same equation and
\[
T^{1,0}M=\ker dR.
\]
Its Levi leaves are the connected components of
\[
R^{-1}(\lambda),\qquad \lambda\in\gamma.
\]

For $\gamma=\mathbb RP^1$ one has
\[
M=\overline{R^{-1}(\mathbb RP^1)},
\]
and, away from the base locus $\{F=G=0\}$,
\[
F\overline G-\overline F\,G=0.
\]
The Levi leaves are
\[
F-\lambda G=0,\qquad \lambda\in\mathbb RP^1.
\]
When $D=\{F=G=0\}$ is irreducible of codimension two and generically
Kupka (hence generically of local product type), this is the basic model for the dicritical configuration in
Theorem~\ref{thm:projective-main}.

The same construction also anticipates the two alternatives for
infinite families of invariant Levi-flats on $\mathbb P^2$. Suppose now that
$n=2$. If two real-analytic curves $\gamma_1,\gamma_2\subset\mathbb P^1$
meet at a regular value $\lambda$, then
\[
\overline{R^{-1}(\gamma_1)}\cap
\overline{R^{-1}(\gamma_2)}
\]
contains the algebraic fiber $R^{-1}(\lambda)$. Thus intersections of
parameter curves produce invariant algebraic leaves. On the other hand,
one may choose infinitely many pairwise disjoint real-analytic curves
in an affine coordinate of the parameter sphere, for example concentric
circles
\[
|z|=r_j,\qquad r_i\ne r_j.
\]
Their inverse images are pairwise separated away from the base locus
and meet there only through the indeterminacy of the pencil. This is the
basic model for the separated pencil-type situation considered in
Section~\ref{sec:many-leviflats-plane}.
head: environment

label: lem:leviflat-transverse-set
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:leviflat-transverse-set}
Let $M\subset X$ be a real-analytic variety of pure real codimension one
invariant by $\mathcal F_\eta$. At every point
\[
p\in M\setminus\bigl(D\cup\operatorname{Sing}(\mathcal F_\eta)\bigr)
\]
there are a neighborhood $U$ of $p$, a holomorphic primitive
\[
F_U:U\longrightarrow\mathbb C,
\qquad dF_U=\eta,
\]
and a real-analytic subset $\gamma_U\subset\mathbb C$ of pure real
dimension one such that
\[
M\cap U=F_U^{-1}(\gamma_U).
\]
Moreover, if $F_V=F_U+c_{UV}, \, c_{UV}\in \mathbb C$ on an overlap $U\cap V \ne \emptyset$, then the corresponding
transverse sets satisfy
\[
\gamma_V=\gamma_U+c_{UV}.
\]
head: environment
name: Invariant Levi-flats and logarithmic transverse structure

title: Proof
body_md:
At a point outside $D\cup\operatorname{Sing}(\mathcal F_\eta)$, the form $\eta$ is
holomorphic and nonvanishing. After shrinking the neighborhood, there is
a holomorphic submersion $F_U$ with $dF_U=\eta$, and its fibers are the
local leaves of $\mathcal F_\eta$.

Since $M$ is invariant, $M\cap U$ is saturated by these fibers. In a
holomorphic flow box this means precisely that $M\cap U$ is the inverse
image of a real-analytic subset of the one-dimensional transverse
parameter. Since $M$ has pure real codimension one, this transverse set
has pure real dimension one. Thus
\[
M\cap U=F_U^{-1}(\gamma_U).
\]
If $F_V=F_U+c_{UV}$ on an overlap, the two descriptions of the same set
$M$ give
\[
F_U^{-1}(\gamma_U)=F_V^{-1}(\gamma_V)
=F_U^{-1}(\gamma_V-c_{UV}),
\]
and therefore
\[
\gamma_V=\gamma_U+c_{UV}.
\]
head: environment

label: lem:period-group-singular-transverse
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:period-group-singular-transverse}
Let
\(
\Gamma=
\left\langle
2\pi i\lambda_1,\ldots,2\pi i\lambda_r
\right\rangle
\subset\mathbb C
\) be the additive subgroup. 
Then the following are equivalent:
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)}]
\item $\Gamma$ is not dense in $\mathbb C$;
\item there exists a nonempty proper closed real-analytic subset
\(
\gamma\subset\mathbb C
\)
of pure real dimension one satisfying
\(
\gamma+\Gamma=\gamma.
\)
\end{enumerate}
Thus no proper $\Gamma$-invariant real-analytic subset of pure real
dimension one exists if and only if
\(
\overline\Gamma=\mathbb C.
\)
head: environment
name: Period groups and singular real-analytic sets

title: Proof
body_md:
Assume first that $\overline\Gamma=\mathbb C$, and let
$\gamma\subset\mathbb C$ be nonempty and closed with
$\gamma+\Gamma=\gamma$. Since translations depend continuously on the
translating parameter,
\[
\gamma+\overline\Gamma=\gamma.
\]
Hence $\gamma+a=\gamma$ for every $a\in\mathbb C$. Choosing
$z_0\in\gamma$ gives $z_0+\mathbb C\subset\gamma$, and therefore
$\gamma=\mathbb C$.

Conversely, suppose that $\Gamma$ is not dense. Its closure is a proper
closed subgroup of the real Lie group
$\mathbb C\simeq\mathbb R^2$. Up to a real-linear change of coordinates,
the possibilities are
\[
\{0\},\qquad
\mathbb Z v,\qquad
\mathbb Z v+\mathbb Z w,\qquad
\mathbb R v,\qquad
\mathbb R v+\mathbb Z w,
\]
where $v$ and $w$ are linearly independent over $\mathbb R$ whenever
both occur.

If the group is contained in a real line $\mathbb R v$, an affine line
parallel to $v$ is invariant. If
\[
\overline\Gamma=\mathbb R v+\mathbb Z w,
\qquad w\notin\mathbb R v,
\]
then
\[
\gamma=
\bigcup_{k\in\mathbb Z}\bigl(\mathbb R v+kw\bigr)
\]
is a proper invariant real-analytic set of pure real dimension one; in
suitable real-linear coordinates it is given by
\[
\sin(\pi y)=0.
\]
If $\overline\Gamma$ is a rank-two lattice, then in lattice coordinates
one may take
\[
\gamma=
\{\sin(\pi x)\sin(\pi y)=0\}.
\]
The trivial and discrete cyclic cases are immediate. Thus every proper
closed subgroup of $\mathbb C$ preserves a proper real-analytic subset
of pure real dimension one.
head: environment

label: prop:period-compatible-leviflats
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:period-compatible-leviflats}
Assume that there exists a nonempty proper real-analytic subset
\[
\gamma\subset\mathbb C
\]
of pure real dimension one satisfying
\[
\gamma+\Gamma=\gamma.
\]
Then the local sets
\[
M_{\gamma,U}=F_U^{-1}(\gamma)
\]
glue on $X^\circ$ to an invariant real-analytic Levi-flat variety
$M_\gamma$. Moreover, the translates $\gamma+c$, $c\in\mathbb C$,
produce infinitely many pairwise distinct invariant Levi-flat varieties
of the same type.

In particular, if $\Gamma$ is not dense in $\mathbb C$, then
$\mathcal F_\eta|_{X^\circ}$ admits infinitely many invariant
real-analytic Levi-flat varieties obtained in this way.
head: environment
name: Period-compatible Levi-flats

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $\{U\}$ be a simply connected covering of $X^\circ$ and choose on
$U$ a primitive $F_U$ of $\eta$. On an overlap one has
\[
F_V=F_U+c_{UV},
\qquad c_{UV}\in\Gamma.
\]
Since $\gamma+\Gamma=\gamma$,
\[
F_V^{-1}(\gamma)
=F_U^{-1}(\gamma-c_{UV})
=F_U^{-1}(\gamma).
\]
Hence the local inverse images glue to a global real-analytic subset
$M_\gamma\subset X^\circ$, saturated by the leaves of
$\mathcal F_\eta$. Its regular part is therefore Levi-flat.

For every $c\in\mathbb C$, the translate $\gamma+c$ is again
$\Gamma$-invariant and gives another global invariant Levi-flat. Since
$\gamma$ is proper, its translation stabilizer
\[
\operatorname{Stab}(\gamma)
=\{c\in\mathbb C;\ \gamma+c=\gamma\}
\]
is a proper closed subgroup of $\mathbb C$. Hence the quotient
$\mathbb C/\operatorname{Stab}(\gamma)$ is infinite, and the family of
translates contains infinitely many distinct members.
The last assertion follows from
Lemma~\ref{lem:period-group-singular-transverse}.
head: environment

title: Remark
body_md:
The converse to Proposition~\ref{prop:period-compatible-leviflats} is
false for arbitrary invariant Levi-flats. Let $R$ be a
nonconstant meromorphic first integral and choose distinct constants
$a_1,\ldots,a_r$. Then
\[
\eta=
\sum_{j=1}^r
\lambda_j\frac{d(R-a_j)}{R-a_j}
=
\left(
\sum_{j=1}^r\frac{\lambda_j}{R-a_j}
\right)dR
\]
defines, away from its polar and zero divisors, the same foliation as
$dR=0$. The coefficients $\lambda_j$ may be chosen so that the period
group of $\eta$ is dense in $\mathbb C$, while the foliation still
admits infinitely many invariant Levi-flat varieties obtained as inverse
images under $R$ of real-analytic curves in $\mathbb P^1$.
head: environment

label: proposition:logarithmic
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{proposition:logarithmic}
Let $\Pi_\eta\subset\mathbb C$ be the actual period group of $\eta$ on
$X^\circ$. For the logarithmic foliation $\mathcal F_\eta$, the
following are equivalent:
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)}]
\item there exists $a\in\mathbb C^*$ such that
\[
\operatorname{Re}(a\tau)=0
\qquad\text{for every }\tau\in\Pi_\eta;
\]
\item after multiplication of $\eta$ by a nonzero constant, the
multivalued primitive has a single-valued real part on $X^\circ$;
\item $\mathcal F_\eta|_{X^\circ}$ admits an infinite one-parameter
family of invariant Levi-flat level hypersurfaces of the form
\[
\{\operatorname{Re}(aF)=c\},
\qquad c\in\mathbb R.
\]
\end{enumerate}
In particular, the collinearity condition
$a\lambda_j\in\mathbb R$ for all $j$ implies these equivalent statements.
When the actual periods are generated by meridians about distinct
reduced polar components with respective residues $\lambda_j$, the
collinearity condition is also necessary.
head: environment
name: Periods and real-part levels

title: Proof
body_md:
The equivalence of \textup{(i)} and \textup{(ii)} follows from the
actual period group. If all periods become purely imaginary after
multiplication by $a$, then $\operatorname{Re}(aF)$ is single-valued and
its regular levels give \textup{(iii)}. Conversely, the expression in
\textup{(iii)} can be globally single-valued only if every period of
$aF$ has zero real part. If $a\lambda_j$ is real for every $j$,
then every period of $a\eta$ is purely imaginary, since the winding
numbers of the functions $f_j$ are integers. Under the final
meridian-generation assumption, the periods $2\pi i\lambda_j$ occur
among the generators, so the same condition is also necessary.
head: environment

label: definition:transvseparation
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{definition:transvseparation}
Let $p$ be a dicritical singularity of $\mathcal F$ contained in an invariant irreducible real-analytic variety of pure real codimension one $M$ with
$\operatorname{Sing}(M)\subset\operatorname{Sing}(\mathcal F)$. Let $U_p$ be a neighborhood of $p$,
let $S$ be a real-analytic one-dimensional manifold, and let
\[
h:M_{\mathrm{reg}}\cap U_p\longrightarrow S
\]
be a real-analytic map on the regular part near $p$. We say that $h$
\emph{separates the nearby Levi leaves at $p$} if $h$ is constant on
each local Levi leaf sufficiently near $p$ and the values assigned to
distinct such leaves are distinct. Equivalently, the induced map on
the set of nearby local Levi leaves is injective. The target $S$ may,
in particular, be $\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb{RP}^1$.
head: environment
name: Separation of nearby Levi leaves

title: Example
body_md:
Consider in $\mathbb C^2$ the local meromorphic first integral
\[
F(x,y)=\frac{x}{y}
\]
and the irreducible real-analytic variety of pure real codimension one 
\[
M=\overline{\left\{(x,y)\in\mathbb C^2;\ y\neq0,\quad
\frac{x}{y}\in\mathbb R\right\}}
=\{x\overline y-\overline x y=0\}.
\]
Its Levi leaves are
\[
L_\lambda=\{x-\lambda y=0\}\cap M_{\mathrm{reg}}
\quad(\lambda\in\mathbb R),\qquad
L_\infty=\{y=0\}\cap M_{\mathrm{reg}},
\]
and the origin is a pencil singularity for $M$. On all of
$M_{\mathrm{reg}}$ near the origin the real-analytic map
\[
h(x,y)=[x:y]\in\mathbb RP^1
\]
is constant on the local pieces of the Levi leaves and satisfies
\[
h|_{L_\lambda}=\lambda.
\]
In the chart $y\neq0$ its real coordinate is
$\operatorname{Re}(x/y)$; the chart $x\neq0$ covers the parameter
$\lambda=\infty$. Thus $h$ separates all nearby Levi leaves. Notice that
$h$ does not extend continuously across the dicritical center $(0,0)$,
as is forced by the pencil-singularity property.
head: environment

label: prop:nearMreg
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:nearMreg}
Let $X$ be a connected complex manifold, let $\mathcal F$ be a codimension-one
holomorphic foliation on $X$, and let $M\subset X$ be a connected irreducible real-analytic variety of pure real codimension one invariant by $\mathcal F$. Let
\[
p\in M\cap\operatorname{Sing}(\mathcal F)
\]
be a pencil singularity for $M$, and let
\[
F_p=\frac{f}{g}:U_p\dashrightarrow\mathbb P^1
\]
be a minimal local meromorphic first integral for the germ $(\mathcal F,p)$.
Then $F_p$ extends by holonomy to a single-valued meromorphic first
integral on an open neighborhood of $M_{\mathrm{reg}}$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Fix $x\in M_{\mathrm{reg}}$ and denote by $L_x$ the Levi leaf through $x$.
By the accumulation hypothesis,
\[
p\in\overline{L_x}.
\]
Hence $L_x$ meets $U_p$.  Choose a regular point
$y\in L_x\cap U_p$ and a path $\gamma\subset L_x$ joining $x$ to
$y$.  Choose small complex transversals $\Sigma_x$ and $\Sigma_y$.
Holonomy along $\gamma$ defines
\[
h_\gamma:\Sigma_x\longrightarrow\Sigma_y.
\]
The meromorphic function
\[
g_\gamma=F_p\circ h_\gamma
\]
on $\Sigma_x$ extends constantly along plaques to a meromorphic first
integral $G_\gamma$ on a flow box around $x$.

Let $\gamma_1,\gamma_2$ be two such choices, and let $G_1,G_2$ be the
corresponding first integrals.  Put
\[
I=\Sigma_x\cap M_{\mathrm{reg}}.
\]
For generic $z\in I$, the two continuations follow the same global
Levi leaf.  By the constancy hypothesis,
\[
G_1(z)=G_2(z)
\]
for generic $z\in I$.  Since $G_1|_{\Sigma_x}$ and
$G_2|_{\Sigma_x}$ are one-variable meromorphic functions and agree on
a real set with an accumulation point,
\[
G_1|_{\Sigma_x}\equiv G_2|_{\Sigma_x}.
\]
Both are constant along plaques, hence $G_1\equiv G_2$ in the flow
box.  The same argument on overlaps gives a meromorphic function
\[
G\in\mathcal M(N_{\mathrm{reg}})
\]
on an open neighborhood $N_{\mathrm{reg}}$ of $M_{\mathrm{reg}}$, and
\[
dG\wedge\omega=0
\]
for every local defining integrable $1$-form $\omega$ of $\mathcal F$.
head: environment

label: def:generic-ltp
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{def:generic-ltp}
Let $D$ be an irreducible component of $\operatorname{Sing}(\mathcal F)$. Following the local
transversely product viewpoint of Lins Neto \cite{LNproduct}, we say that
$D$ is \emph{generically of local product type} if there exists a proper
complex-analytic subset
\[
E_D\subsetneq D,
\qquad \operatorname{Sing}(D)\subset E_D,
\]
such that
\[
D^\circ:=D\setminus E_D
\]
is connected and dense, and there exists a fixed germ $\mathcal G$ of a
singular foliation in a transverse two-dimensional space such that, near
every point of $D^\circ$, the foliation $\mathcal F$ is analytically the pull-back
of $\mathcal G$ by a submersion. We call $D^\circ$ the generic
local-product locus and $E_D$ the exceptional locus.
head: environment
name: Generic local product type

label: lem:product-propagation
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:product-propagation}
Let $L\subset M_{\mathrm{reg}}$ be a Levi leaf. If
\[
\overline L\cap D^\circ\neq\varnothing,
\]
then
\[
D^\circ\subset\overline L.
\]
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Set $S_L=\overline L\cap D^\circ$. It is closed in $D^\circ$. Let
$q\in S_L$. In local-product coordinates near $q$, the foliation is the
product of its fixed transverse germ with the regular foliation along
$D^\circ$. Since $L$ accumulates at $q$, the closure of the corresponding
local leaf contains the whole local plaque of $D^\circ$ through $q$.
Hence $S_L$ is open in $D^\circ$. Since $D^\circ$ is connected,
$S_L=D^\circ$.
head: environment

label: lem:monodromy
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:monodromy}
Let $D$ be an irreducible dicritical component which is generically of
local product type, let $D^\circ$ be its connected generic local-product
locus, and fix $p\in D^\circ$. Suppose that a minimal local meromorphic first integral
\[
F_p:U_p\dashrightarrow\mathbb P^1
\]
has the property that, for every generic global Levi leaf $L$
represented near $p$, the restriction $F_p|_{L\cap U_p}$ is constant. Then the projective
monodromy of the transverse $\mathbb P^1$-parameter along $D^\circ$ is trivial.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Normalize the parameter at $p$ by $H_p=F_p$.  Analytic continuation
around a loop $\gamma\in\pi_1(D^\circ,p)$ gives an element
\[
\rho(\gamma)\in\operatorname{PGL}(2,\mathbb C).
\]
For a generic Levi leaf $L$ represented near $p$, let
\[
\lambda(L)=H_p(L).
\]
After continuation around $\gamma$, the same leaf is assigned the
parameter $\rho(\gamma)(\lambda(L))$.  The constancy hypothesis at $p$ gives
\[
\rho(\gamma)(\lambda(L))=\lambda(L)
\]
for every generic Levi leaf.  The local Levi-flat supplies infinitely
many such parameters with an accumulation point.  A nonidentity
M\"obius transformation has at most two fixed points.  Therefore
$\rho(\gamma)=\operatorname{id}$ for every $\gamma$, as claimed.
head: environment

label: def:no-degree-jump
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{def:no-degree-jump}
We say that the generic transverse parameter along $D^\circ$ has
\emph{no transverse degree jump along $D$} if, for every
$q\in D\setminus D^\circ$ and every minimal local meromorphic first
integral
\[
H_q:U_q\dashrightarrow\mathbb P^1
\]
of the germ $(\mathcal F,q)$, the restriction of $H_q$ near a generic point
$r\in D^\circ\cap U_q$ is still minimal. Equivalently, if
$\widehat H_r$ is a normalized minimal transverse parameter at such an
$r$ and
\[
H_q=R_q\circ\widehat H_r,
\]
then $\deg R_q=1$.
head: environment
name: No transverse degree jump

label: prop:dicritical-extension
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:dicritical-extension}
The meromorphic first integral $G$ constructed in
Proposition~\ref{prop:nearMreg} extends meromorphically through every
point of $D^\circ$. If, in addition, the no-transverse-degree-jump
condition of Definition~\ref{def:no-degree-jump} holds, then $G$
extends meromorphically through every point of $D$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $q\in D^\circ$. On the nonempty overlap of $U_q$ with
$N_{\mathrm{reg}}$ the functions $G$ and $\widehat H_q$ are first integrals
of the same foliation and have the same values on generic Levi leaves.
Hence they agree. Since $\widehat H_q$ is meromorphic on $U_q$, it
extends $G$ through $q$.

Now let $q\in D\setminus D^\circ$ and assume the no-transverse-degree-jump
condition. By the local theorem of Cerveau--Lins Neto there is a minimal
local meromorphic first integral
\[
H_q:U_q\dashrightarrow\mathbb P^1.
\]
Choose a generic point $r\in D^\circ\cap U_q$. By hypothesis the
restriction of $H_q$ near $r$ is minimal. Since $\widehat H_r$ is also
minimal, the two first integrals differ by a M\"obius transformation:
\[
\widehat H_r=A_q\circ H_q,
\qquad A_q\in\operatorname{PGL}(2,\mathbb C).
\]
The function $A_q\circ H_q$ is meromorphic on $U_q$ and agrees with
$G$ on a nonempty open set. Uniqueness of meromorphic continuation
therefore gives the extension through $q$.
head: environment

label: ex:degree-jump
title: Example
body_md:
\label{ex:degree-jump}
The condition in Definition~\ref{def:no-degree-jump} is not automatic.
Let $d\ge2$ and consider in $(\mathbb C^3,0)$ the meromorphic first integral
\[
H(x,y,z)=\frac{x^d}{y^d z}.
\]
The associated foliation is defined, after clearing denominators, by
\[
\omega=d yz\,dx-d xz\,dy-xy\,dz,
\]
and its singular set contains
\[
D=\{x=y=0\}.
\]
At $q=(0,0,0)$ the first integral $H$ is primitive:  For a generic $c\in\mathbb C^*$, the fiber germ
\[
x^d-cy^dz=0
\]
is irreducible. Indeed, viewed as a polynomial in $x$ over
$\mathbb C\{y,z\}$, it satisfies Eisenstein's criterion with respect to
the prime element $z$ \cite[\S 9.4]{DummitFoote}. On the other hand, at a nearby point
$p=(0,0,z_0)\in D$, $z_0\ne0$, choose a holomorphic branch
$a(z)$ with $a(z)^d=z$. Then
\[
G_p(x,y,z)=\frac{x}{a(z)y}
\]
is a primitive local meromorphic first integral and
\[
H=G_p^d.
\]
Thus a primitive first integral at the exceptional point $q$ restricts
near generic points of $D$ as a nonprimitive degree-$d$ quotient.
head: environment
name: A genuine transverse degree jump

label: lem:nondicritical
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Since $q$ is non-dicritical, a minimal local meromorphic first integral
has no indeterminacy at $q$: otherwise a reduced representation $f/g$
with $f(q)=g(q)=0$ would produce infinitely many distinct local
separatrices through $q$. After shrinking $U_q$ and choosing the
appropriate target chart, we may therefore take a minimal holomorphic
first integral
\[
H_q:U_q\longrightarrow\mathbb C,\qquad H_q(q)=c.
\]
On the regular locus of $H_q$, invariance of $M$ means that $M$ is
saturated by the level hypersurfaces of $H_q$. Hence the image of the
regular part of the relevant local component of $M$ in the one-dimensional
leaf space is a real-analytic curve germ. After selecting that component,
there is a germ of a real-analytic curve $\gamma\subset\mathbb C$, with
$c\in\gamma$, such that
\[
M\cap U_q=\overline{H_q^{-1}(\gamma)}.
\]
In particular,
\[
H_q^{-1}(c)\subset M.
\]

The fiber $H_q^{-1}(c)$ is a complex hypersurface through $q$. Since
$\operatorname{Sing}(\mathcal F)$ has complex codimension at least two, it is not contained
in $\operatorname{Sing}(\mathcal F)$. We may therefore choose
\[
x\in H_q^{-1}(c)\cap M,
\qquad x\notin\operatorname{Sing}(\mathcal F),
\]
arbitrarily close to $q$. Since $\operatorname{Sing}(M)\subset\operatorname{Sing}(\mathcal F)$, we have
$x\in M_{\mathrm{reg}}$.

Near $x$, both $G$ and $H_q$ are first integrals of the same regular
codimension-one foliation. Since $H_q(x)=c$, there exists a one-variable
meromorphic germ $\varphi$ at $c$ such that
\[
G=\varphi\circ H_q
\]
on a neighborhood of $x$. Therefore $\varphi\circ H_q$ is meromorphic
near $q$ and agrees with $G$ on a nonempty open subset of their common
domain. By uniqueness of meromorphic continuation, it extends $G$
through $q$.
head: environment

label: thm:semiglobal
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:semiglobal}
Let $X$ be a connected complex manifold of dimension $n\ge3$, let $\mathcal F$ be a
codimension-one holomorphic foliation on $X$, and let $M\subset X$ be
a connected irreducible real-analytic variety of pure real codimension one  invariant
by $\mathcal F$. Assume:

\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)}]
\item
\[
\operatorname{Sing}(M)\subset\operatorname{Sing}(\mathcal F);
\]

\item all dicritical singularities of $\mathcal F$ contained in $M$ belong to
an irreducible codimension-two complex analytic subset
\[
D\subset M\cap\operatorname{Sing}(\mathcal F),
\]
and $D$ is generically of local product type;

\item there exists a pencil singularity for $M$ in the local-product
locus of $D$;

\item the generic transverse parameter along $D^\circ$ has no
transverse degree jump along $D$ in the sense of
Definition~\ref{def:no-degree-jump}.
\end{enumerate}

Then there exist an open neighborhood $N\supset M$ and a nonconstant
meromorphic first integral
\[
G\in\mathcal M(N)
\]
for $\mathcal F|_N$.
head: environment
name: Semi-global integrability

title: Proof
body_md:
Proposition~\ref{prop:nearMreg} gives a meromorphic first integral near
$M_{\mathrm{reg}}$. By hypothesis 	extup{(iv)},
Proposition~\ref{prop:dicritical-extension} extends it through the
whole dicritical component $D$, while Lemma~\ref{lem:nondicritical}
extends it through the remaining points
of $M\cap\operatorname{Sing}(\mathcal F)$.  Since
\[
\operatorname{Sing}(M)\subset\operatorname{Sing}(\mathcal F),
\]
these extensions cover all points of $M$.  By uniqueness of
meromorphic continuation they glue to a nonconstant meromorphic first
integral
\[
G\in\mathcal M(N)
\]
on some open neighborhood $N\supset M$.
head: environment

label: prop:pseudoconvex
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:pseudoconvex}
Let $X$ be a connected complex manifold and let $M\subset X$ be a singular Levi-flat variety. Assume that, near every point $q\in M$, the Levi foliation is defined by a local meromorphic first integral. Then every local side of $M$ is pseudoconvex, including at singular points of $M$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Since $M$ has pure real codimension one, its smooth hypersurface locus
is dense in $M$. By Lebl's complex-leaf lemma
\cite[Lemma~5.4]{LeblSingularSet}, through every $q\in M$ there is a
germ of a complex hypersurface contained in $M$. Let $h_q$ be a
holomorphic equation for this hypersurface on a small coordinate
neighborhood. The germ $1/h_q$ is holomorphic on each local component
of the complement of $M$ and cannot extend holomorphically across
$q$. The local characterization of pseudoconvexity by domains of
holomorphy gives the conclusion, including at singular points.
head: environment

label: lem:boundary-hartogs
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:boundary-hartogs}
Let $Y$ be a compact complex manifold, let $M\subset Y$ be compact, and
let $\Omega$ be a connected component of $Y\setminus M$. Assume that
$\Omega$ is Stein and $\dim_\mathbb C\Omega\ge2$. Let $N$ be an open
neighborhood of $M$ in $Y$ and let
\[
g\in\mathcal M(N\cap\Omega).
\]
Then there are a smaller neighborhood $N'\subset N$ of $M$ and a
meromorphic function
\[
\widetilde g\in\mathcal M(\Omega)
\]
such that
\[
\widetilde g=g\qquad\text{on }N'\cap\Omega.
\]
head: environment
name: Hartogs extension from a boundary neighborhood

title: Proof
body_md:
Since $Y$ is compact and $N$ contains $\partial\Omega\subset M$, the set
$\Omega\setminus N$ is relatively compact in $\Omega$. A connected
Stein manifold of complex dimension at least two has only one end; see,
for instance, Serre \cite{SerreDuality}. Hence there exists a compact set
$K\Subset\Omega$ containing $\Omega\setminus N$ such that
\[
\Omega\setminus K
\]
is connected. In particular,
\[
\Omega\setminus K\subset N\cap\Omega.
\]
The meromorphic Hartogs theorem
\cite[Theorem~2.2]{MerkerPorten} extends
$g|_{\Omega\setminus K}$ meromorphically to all of $\Omega$; denote the
extension by $\widetilde g$.

Since $K$ is compact and disjoint from $M$, we may shrink $N$ to a
neighborhood $N'\subset N$ of $M$ such that $N'\cap K=\varnothing$.
Then
\[
N'\cap\Omega\subset\Omega\setminus K,
\]
so $\widetilde g=g$ on $N'\cap\Omega$, as claimed.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $p\in D^\circ$ be the pencil singularity in hypothesis
\textup{(iii)}. By Proposition~\ref{prop:nearMreg}, the corresponding
minimal local parameter extends by holonomy to a single-valued
meromorphic first integral
\[
G\in\mathcal M(N_{\mathrm{reg}})
\]
on an open neighborhood $N_{\mathrm{reg}}$ of $M_{\mathrm{reg}}$. By
Lemma~\ref{lem:monodromy}, the projective transverse monodromy along
$D^\circ$ is trivial; hence the local minimal first integrals along
$D^\circ$ may be normalized as $\widehat H_q$, $q\in D^\circ$, so as
to agree with $G$ wherever both are defined.

By the analytic exceptional-locus condition in Definition~\ref{def:generic-ltp},
we have
\[
E_D=D\setminus D^\circ,
\qquad \dim_\mathbb C E_D\le n-3.
\]
Choose a generic linear plane
\[
P\simeq\mathbb P^2\subset\mathbb P^n
\]
such that
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\alph*)}]
\item $P\cap E_D=\varnothing$ and $P$ is transverse to $D^\circ$;
\item $P$ is transverse to $M_{\mathrm{reg}}$ at every point of
$P\cap M_{\mathrm{reg}}$;
\item $P$ is in general position with $\mathcal F$: it is not invariant and
its tangency locus with $\mathcal F$ has codimension at least two in $P$;
\item the restriction $\mathcal F_P:=\mathcal F|_P$ is a codimension-one foliation on
$P$, and at every point of $P\cap(M\cap\operatorname{Sing}(\mathcal F))$ outside $D$ the
restriction to $P$ of a local holomorphic first integral is nonconstant.
\end{enumerate}
Here is a direct justification of condition \textup{(b)}. Let
$\mathcal G=\operatorname{Gr}(3,n+1)$ be the Grassmannian of projective
two-planes, of real dimension $6n-12$. At a fixed point
$x\in M_{\mathrm{reg}}$, nontransversality is equivalent to
\[
T_xP\subset T_x^{\mathbb C}M,
\]
since $T_xP$ is complex and $T_x^{\mathbb C}M$ is the maximal complex
subspace of the real hyperplane $T_xM$. The tangent directions of
such planes through $x$ form $\operatorname{Gr}(2,n-1)$, of real
dimension $4(n-3)$. The incidence space of nontransverse pairs
$(x,P)$ therefore has real dimension
\[
(2n-1)+4(n-3)=6n-13<\dim_{\mathbb R}\mathcal G.
\]
By Sard's theorem its image has measure zero. Thus a plane can be
chosen transverse to $M_{\mathrm{reg}}$ at every point of intersection.
Condition \textup{(c)} holds on a Zariski open dense set of planes
\cite[Theorem~3.25]{CerveauLinsNetoStructural}; the remaining
conditions are obtained by the usual generic linear-section choices.
In particular, these requirements can be imposed simultaneously. Then
\[
P\cap D=\{q_1,\ldots,q_s\}\subset D^\circ.
\]
Put
\[
M_P=M\cap P,
\qquad G_P=G|_{P\cap N_{\mathrm{reg}}}.
\]
The function $G_P$ is a meromorphic first integral for $\mathcal F_P$ near
$P\cap M_{\mathrm{reg}}$.

At each $q_j$, transversality of $P$ to $D$ identifies the germ of
$\mathcal F_P$ with the fixed two-dimensional transverse germ of the
local-product structure. Consequently
\[
H_j:=\widehat H_{q_j}|_P
\]
is a minimal local meromorphic first integral of $\mathcal F_P$ at $q_j$.
By the normalization along $D^\circ$, $H_j$ agrees with $G_P$ on a
nonempty open subset of their common domain. Hence $H_j$ extends
$G_P$ meromorphically through $q_j$. In particular, the several
dicritical points of the plane section are automatically compatible;
with the inherited normalization all transition maps are the identity.

Let now $a\in M_P\cap\operatorname{Sing}(\mathcal F_P)$ with $a\notin P\cap D$.
Condition \textup{(b)} excludes tangencies of $P$ with the regular ambient
foliation at points of $M_{\mathrm{reg}}$, because
$T_a\mathcal F=T_a^{\mathbb C}M$ there. Hence such a point $a$ lies in
$M\cap\operatorname{Sing}(\mathcal F)$ outside $D$, and is nondicritical by hypothesis
\textup{(ii)} of Theorem~\ref{thm:projective-main}. By the genericity
condition \textup{(d)}, a local holomorphic first integral restricts
nontrivially to $P$. The two-dimensional form of
Lemma~\ref{lem:nondicritical} therefore extends $G_P$ through $a$.
Thus $G_P$ extends to a nonconstant meromorphic first integral on a
neighborhood $N_P$ of $M_P$ in $P$.

Let $\Omega$ be a connected component of $P\setminus M_P$.
Proposition~\ref{prop:pseudoconvex} shows that $\Omega$ is locally
pseudoconvex in $P$, and Takeuchi's theorem
\cite[Theorem~IV, p.~181]{Takeuchi} implies that $\Omega$ is Stein.
Lemma~\ref{lem:boundary-hartogs}, applied to
$G_P|_{N_P\cap\Omega}$, extends $G_P$ meromorphically through $\Omega$
after shrinking $N_P$ near $M_P$. Repeating this for the finitely many
components of $P\setminus M_P$ and shrinking once more if necessary,
the extensions glue with $G_P$ on a neighborhood of $M_P$. We obtain a
global meromorphic function on $P\simeq\mathbb P^2$, hence a nonconstant
rational first integral of $\mathcal F_P$.

Finally, the extension statement in
\cite[Theorem~3.25]{CerveauLinsNetoStructural} applies to the plane
$P$, which is in general position with $\mathcal F$ by condition
\textup{(c)}: the rational first integral of $\mathcal F_P$ extends to a
rational first integral of $\mathcal F$ on $\mathbb P^n$. This completes the proof.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $\gamma_p\subset\mathbb P^1$ be the set of parameters of the local Levi
leaves represented in $M_{\mathrm{reg}}\cap U_p$. Since $h$ is constant on local Levi leaves
and the generic fibers of the minimal parameter $F_p$ are connected,
it induces a map $\eta:\gamma_p\longrightarrow S$ with
\[
h=\eta\circ F_p
\]
on generic local leaves. The assumption that $h$ separates the nearby
Levi leaves means that $\eta$ is injective on the entire relevant
transverse parameter set, including when it is a circle.

Let a generic global Levi leaf $L$ have two sufficiently near-$p$
components contained respectively in $V_{\lambda_1}$ and
$V_{\lambda_2}$. By the global-leaf compatibility assumed for $h$,
\[
\eta(\lambda_1)=h|_{L\cap U_p}=\eta(\lambda_2).
\]
Hence $\lambda_1=\lambda_2$. By
Lemma~\ref{lem:product-propagation}, the assumption that each Levi leaf
accumulates at some point of the local-product locus gives
\[
p\in\overline L
\]
for every Levi leaf $L\subset M_{\mathrm{reg}}$. Together with the uniqueness of
the local parameter proved above, this shows that $p$ is a pencil
singularity for $M$. Theorem~\ref{thm:projective-main} now gives the
conclusion.
head: environment

label: lem:real-transverse
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:real-transverse}
Assume that $\mathcal F\subset\mathcal H$. Then  the holonomy pseudogroup of $\mathcal F$ acting on the transverse parameter defined by $\mathcal F$
 preserve the real one-dimensional foliation induced by
$\mathcal H$ on a complex transversal. In particular, whenever minimal
local meromorphic first integrals identify the transverse leaf space
with $\mathbb P^1$, the corresponding projective monodromy is contained in
the subgroup of $\operatorname{PGL}(2,\mathbb C)$ preserving that real
foliation.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
At a regular point of $\mathcal F$, choose a local holomorphic first integral
$f_i$ on a flow box. Since $\mathcal F\subset\mathcal H$, the foliation $\mathcal H$
descends to a real one-dimensional foliation on the complex
transversal parametrized by $f_i$. On an overlap,
\[
f_j=\varphi_{ij}(f_i)
\]
for a holomorphic change of transverse coordinate. Since $\mathcal H$ is
globally defined, $\varphi_{ij}$ sends leaves of the induced real
foliation in the $f_i$-plane to leaves of the induced real foliation
in the $f_j$-plane. This proves the first assertion.

When minimal meromorphic first integrals identify the local transverse
leaf spaces with $\mathbb P^1$, the corresponding projective transition
maps therefore belong to the subgroup of
$\operatorname{PGL}(2,\mathbb C)$ preserving the induced real foliation.
head: environment

label: lem:transverse-rigidity
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:transverse-rigidity}
Let
\[
G\subset\operatorname{Diff}(\mathbb C,0)
\]
be a group of germs of holomorphic diffeomorphisms. Assume that there
exists an infinite family
\[
\{\gamma_\alpha\}_{\alpha\in A}
\]
of pairwise distinct smooth real-analytic curve germs through the
origin such that
\[
g(\gamma_\alpha)=\gamma_\alpha
\]
for every $g\in G$ and every $\alpha\in A$. Then $G$ is abelian.
head: environment
name: Transverse rigidity

title: Proof
body_md:
For a smooth real-analytic curve germ $\gamma\subset(\mathbb C,0)$, denote by
$\sigma_\gamma$ the Schwarz reflection across $\gamma$.  Thus
$\sigma_\gamma$ is the antiholomorphic involution fixing $\gamma$
pointwise.  If $\phi$ is a local holomorphic coordinate straightening
$\gamma$ to $\mathbb R$, then
\[
\sigma_\gamma=\phi^{-1}\circ c\circ\phi,
\qquad c(z)=\overline z.
\]
If $g\in\operatorname{Diff}(\mathbb C,0)$ preserves $\gamma$, then
$g\sigma_\gamma g^{-1}$ is again the antiholomorphic involution fixing
$\gamma$ pointwise.  By uniqueness of Schwarz reflection,
\[
g\circ\sigma_\gamma=\sigma_\gamma\circ g.
\tag{\ref{lem:transverse-rigidity}.1}
\]
Hence every element of $G$ commutes with every reflection associated
with the family.

We distinguish two cases.

Suppose first that the set of tangent lines
\[
\{T_0\gamma_\alpha:\alpha\in A\}
\]
is infinite. Since any $g\in G$ preserves one such real tangent line,
its multiplier is real:
\[
g'(0)\in\mathbb R^*.
\]
If some $f\in G$ has $|f'(0)|\ne1$, then $f$ is analytically
linearizable. In a linearizing coordinate we may write
\[
f(z)=\lambda z,
\qquad \lambda\in\mathbb R^*,\quad |\lambda|\ne1.
\]
Every smooth real-analytic $f$-invariant curve through the origin is a
straight real line. Indeed, after a rotation, and after replacing $f$
by a suitable iterate or inverse, write the curve as
\[
y=\varphi(x),\qquad 0<\lambda<1,
\]
with $\varphi(0)=\varphi'(0)=0$. Invariance gives
\[
\varphi(\lambda x)=\lambda\varphi(x).
\]
Writing $\varphi(x)=\sum_{j\ge2}a_jx^j$ yields
$a_j(\lambda^j-\lambda)=0$, and therefore $\varphi\equiv0$.
Consequently our family contains infinitely many distinct real lines
\[
L_\theta=e^{i\theta}\mathbb R.
\]
If
\[
g(z)=\sum_{j\ge1}b_jz^j\in G,
\]
then $g(L_\theta)=L_\theta$ implies
\[
b_je^{i(j-1)\theta}\in\mathbb R
\]
for every $j$ and infinitely many values of $\theta$ modulo $\pi$.
For $j\ge2$ this forces $b_j=0$. Hence every element of $G$ is a real
homothety, and $G$ is abelian.

It remains, in the present case, to assume that $|g'(0)|=1$ for every
$g\in G$. Since all multipliers are real,
\[
g'(0)\in\{1,-1\}.
\]
If $g'(0)=1$ and $g\ne\operatorname{id}$, write
\[
g(z)=z+az^{k+1}+O(z^{k+2}),
\qquad a\ne0.
\]
Let $\gamma$ be a smooth real-analytic invariant curve with tangent
vector $v\ne0$, and write
\[
\gamma(t)=vt+O(t^2),
\qquad
g(\gamma(t))=\gamma(\rho(t)).
\]
Comparison at the first nonlinear order gives
\[
av^k\in\mathbb R.
\]
Thus a nontrivial germ tangent to the identity admits invariant smooth
real-analytic curves in only finitely many tangent directions, contrary
to the present hypothesis. Hence $g'(0)=1$ implies
$g=\operatorname{id}$. If $g'(0)=-1$, then $(g^2)'(0)=1$, so
$g^2=\operatorname{id}$. Moreover, if $g$ and $h$ both have multiplier
$-1$, then $(gh)'(0)=1$, whence $gh=\operatorname{id}$ and $g=h$.
Thus $G$ has at most two elements and is again abelian.

Suppose now that only finitely many tangent directions occur. Since the
family is infinite, there are two distinct curves $\gamma_1$ and
$\gamma_2$ with
\[
T_0\gamma_1=T_0\gamma_2.
\]
Let $\sigma_1$ and $\sigma_2$ be their Schwarz reflections and set
\[
F=\sigma_2\circ\sigma_1.
\]
Then $F$ is holomorphic and $F'(0)=1$. Moreover $F$ is not the
identity, since otherwise $\sigma_1=\sigma_2$ and therefore
$\gamma_1=\gamma_2$. Hence
\[
F(z)=z+az^{k+1}+\cdots,
\qquad a\ne0.
\]
By \textup{(\ref{lem:transverse-rigidity}.1)}, every element of $G$
commutes with both $\sigma_1$ and $\sigma_2$, and therefore
\[
G\subset Z(F),
\]
where $Z(F)$ denotes the centralizer of $F$ in
$\operatorname{Diff}(\mathbb C,0)$.

We recall the standard formal argument showing that $Z(F)$ is abelian.
There is a unique formal vector field
\[
X=\log F
\]
with $F=\exp X$. If $gF=Fg$, then
\[
g_*X=X.
\]
Writing
\[
X=a(z)\frac{\partial}{\partial z},
\]
consider the formal meromorphic differential
\[
\omega=\frac{dz}{a(z)}.
\]
The identity $g_*X=X$ is equivalent to $g^*\omega=\omega$. If $T$ is a
formal primitive of $\omega$, then for every $g\in Z(F)$ one has
\[
T\circ g=T+c_g
\]
for some constant $c_g$. Therefore, for $g,h\in Z(F)$,
\[
T\circ g\circ h=T+c_h+c_g
=T+c_g+c_h=T\circ h\circ g.
\]
Since $T$ is a nonconstant formal Fatou coordinate, this implies
$g\circ h=h\circ g$. Thus $Z(F)$, and hence $G$, is abelian.

label: lem:abelian-invariant-form
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:abelian-invariant-form}
Let
\[
G\subset\operatorname{Diff}(\mathbb C,0)
\]
be an abelian group. Then there exists a nonzero formal meromorphic
$1$-form $\widehat\omega$ at the origin such that
\[
g^*\widehat\omega=\widehat\omega
\qquad\text{for every }g\in G.
\]
head: environment
name: Invariant formal transverse differential

title: Proof
body_md:
If $G$ is formally linearizable, choose a formal coordinate $z$ in
which every element is a homothety. Then
\[
\widehat\omega=\frac{dz}{z}
\]
is invariant by every element in $G$. Otherwise $G$ contains a non-periodic element tangent to
the identity after taking a suitable iterate. Write this element as
\[
g_0=\exp \hat {\mathcal Z},
\qquad
\hat {\mathcal Z}=a(z)\frac{\partial}{\partial z},
\]
for some formal one-variable vector field $\hat {\mathcal Z}$ with $\hat {\mathcal Z}\ne0$. Since $G$ is abelian, every  $g \in G$ commutes with
$g_0$, hence preserves the unique formal logarithm $\hat {\mathcal Z}$. Therefore it
preserves
\[
\widehat\omega=\frac{dz}{a(z)}.
\]
head: environment

label: lem:closed-rational-logarithmic
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:closed-rational-logarithmic}
Let $\mathcal F$ be a holomorphic foliation on $\mathbb P^2$ defined by a
closed rational $1$-form. Assume that the reduction of singularities of
$\mathcal F$ contains no saddle-nodes. Then $\mathcal F$ is defined by a
closed logarithmic rational $1$-form.
head: environment
name: Closed rational forms without saddle-nodes are logarithmic

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $\omega$ be a closed rational $1$-form defining $\mathcal F$. Write
\[
\omega=\alpha+dR,
\]
where $\alpha$ is logarithmic and
\(
R\in\mathbb C(\mathbb P^2).
\)
If $R$ is constant, there is nothing to prove. Also, if $\mathcal F$
admits a rational first integral $H$, then
\[
\frac{dH}{H}
\]
is a closed logarithmic $1$-form defining the same foliation. We may
therefore assume, seeking a contradiction, that $R$ is nonconstant and
that $\mathcal F$ admits no rational first integral.

Start with a reduction of singularities of $\mathcal F$. By hypothesis
all its reduced singularities are nondegenerate. Further point blow-ups
do not create saddle-nodes: blowing up a regular point produces at worst
a reduced nondegenerate singularity, and blowing up a reduced
nondegenerate singularity whose eigenvalue quotient is not a positive
rational again produces only reduced nondegenerate singularities. Thus
the absence of saddle-nodes persists under any additional blow-ups.

We may therefore resolve simultaneously the remaining indeterminacy of
$R$ and the polar divisor of $\alpha$:
\[
\pi:S\longrightarrow\mathbb P^2,
\]
in such a way that
\[
f:=R\circ\pi:S\longrightarrow\mathbb P^1
\]
is a holomorphic map and the relevant divisors have normal crossings.
We have
\[
\pi^*\omega=\widetilde\alpha+df,
\qquad
\widetilde\alpha=\pi^*\alpha,
\]
with $\widetilde\alpha$ logarithmic.

We claim that every irreducible component of the polar divisor of
$\widetilde\alpha$ is vertical with respect to $f$. Suppose, on the
contrary, that $H$ is a horizontal polar component. Then $H$ meets the
fiber
\[
f^{-1}(\infty).
\]
After the above resolution, choose a point
\[
p\in H\cap f^{-1}(\infty)
\]
at which $H$ meets a unique irreducible component of that fiber. In
suitable local coordinates centered at $p$,
\[
f=x^{-m},
\qquad
H=\{y=0\},
\qquad m\geq1,
\]
and
\[
\widetilde\alpha=
\lambda\frac{dy}{y}
+\mu\frac{dx}{x}
+\beta,
\qquad
\lambda\neq0,
\]
where $\beta$ is holomorphic. Hence
\[
\pi^*\omega
=
-mx^{-m-1}\,dx
+\lambda\frac{dy}{y}
+\mu\frac{dx}{x}
+\beta.
\]
Multiplying by $x^{m+1}y$, which does not change the foliation, gives a
holomorphic $1$-form of the shape
\[
\Omega=
\bigl(-my+\text{higher order terms}\bigr)\,dx
+
\bigl(\lambda x^{m+1}+\text{higher order terms}\bigr)\,dy.
\]
Its associated vector field has one zero eigenvalue and one nonzero
eigenvalue. Thus $p$ is a saddle-node, contradicting the hypothesis.
Therefore all polar components of $\widetilde\alpha$ are vertical.

Let
\[
\operatorname{Res}(\widetilde\alpha)
=
\sum_a D_a,
\]
where each divisor $D_a$ is supported on the fiber $f^{-1}(a)$. Since
$\widetilde\alpha$ is a global closed logarithmic form, its residue
divisor has trivial Chern class. Therefore, for every irreducible
component $C$ of $f^{-1}(a)$,
\[
D_a\cdot C=0.
\]
By Zariski's lemma, the intersection matrix of the irreducible
components of a fiber is negative semidefinite and its kernel is
generated by the multiplicity vector of the whole fiber. Consequently,
for every $a$,
\[
D_a=c_a\,f^{-1}(a)
\]
for some $c_a\in\mathbb C$.

Since all fibers of $f$ are numerically equivalent and the total
residue divisor has trivial Chern class, one also has
\[
\sum_a c_a=0.
\]
Hence there exists a logarithmic $1$-form $\beta_0$ on $\mathbb P^1$
with residue divisor
\[
\sum_a c_a[a].
\]
Then
\[
\widetilde\alpha-f^*\beta_0
\]
has zero residues and hence is holomorphic on $S$. Since $S$ is a
rational surface,
\[
H^0(S,\Omega_S^1)=0,
\]
and therefore
\[
\widetilde\alpha=f^*\beta_0.
\]
It follows that
\[
\pi^*\omega
=
df+f^*\beta_0
=
f^*(dt+\beta_0).
\]
Hence the transformed foliation is tangent to the fibers of $f$, so
$f$ is a rational first integral of $\pi^*\mathcal F$. Thus $R$ is a
rational first integral of $\mathcal F$, contradicting our assumption.

Therefore either $R$ is constant, in which case $\omega$ is
logarithmic, or $\mathcal F$ admits a rational first integral, in which
case it is defined by a logarithmic form of the type $dH/H$. In either
case $\mathcal F$ is logarithmic.
head: environment

title: Definition
body_md:
Let $L$ be a leaf of $\mathcal F$, let $q\in L$, and let
$\Sigma$ be a small transversal to $\mathcal F$ through $q$.
The virtual holonomy group of $L$ with respect to $\Sigma$ is
\[
\operatorname{Hol}^{\mathrm{virt}}(\mathcal F,L,\Sigma,q)
=
\left\{
h\in\operatorname{Diff}(\Sigma,q)\,;\,
L_z=L_{h(z)}
\ \text{for every }z\in(\Sigma,q)
\right\},
\]
where $L_z$ denotes the leaf of $\mathcal F$ through $z$.
Equivalently, it consists of the germs of local transverse
biholomorphisms fixing $q$ and preserving each leaf of the foliation.
head: environment
name: virtual holonomy

label: prop:many-leviflats-holonomy
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:many-leviflats-holonomy}
Let $\mathcal F$ be a codimension-one holomorphic foliation on a complex
manifold $X$, let $L$ be a regular leaf, and fix $q\in L$. Assume that
there is an infinite family $\{M_\alpha\}_{\alpha\in A}$ of invariant
real-analytic Levi-flat variety germs, smooth along $L$, pairwise distinct
near $q$, such that $L\subset M_\alpha$ for every $\alpha$. Then the
virtual holonomy group of $L$ at $q$ is abelian. In particular, the
ordinary holonomy group is abelian.
head: environment
name: Virtual holonomy rigidity from many Levi-flats

title: Proof
body_md:
Choose a sufficiently small complex transversal
\[
(\Sigma,q)\simeq(\mathbb C,0)
\]
to $L$. Since each $M_\alpha$ is real analytic, Levi-flat and saturated
by $\mathcal F$, its intersection with $\Sigma$ is a smooth real-analytic curve
germ
\[
\gamma_\alpha=M_\alpha\cap\Sigma.
\]
In a foliated flow box a saturated hypersurface germ is completely
determined by its transverse trace. Hence the pairwise distinct germs
$M_\alpha$ give pairwise distinct germs $\gamma_\alpha$.

Let $h$ belong to the virtual holonomy group. By definition, $h(z)$ is
on the same local leaf as $z$. Since every $M_\alpha$ is saturated, a
point $z\in\gamma_\alpha$ and every point on its local leaf belong to
$M_\alpha$. Hence
\[
h(\gamma_\alpha)=\gamma_\alpha
\]
for every $\alpha$. Lemma~\ref{lem:transverse-rigidity} applies to the
whole virtual holonomy group and proves that it is abelian.
head: environment

label: rem:many-leviflats-local
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{rem:many-leviflats-local}
The proposition is local along the leaf. In particular, it does not
require the ambient manifold to be compact, nor does it require the
foliation to be nonsingular away from the chosen regular leaf. The
essential hypotheses are the existence of infinitely many distinct
invariant real-analytic Levi-flat germs containing the same leaf and
the resulting common family of invariant transverse curves.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Fix infinitely many members $M_\alpha$ satisfying \textup{(H)} and put
\[
X_\alpha=(M_0\cap M_\alpha)\setminus\operatorname{Sing}(\mathcal F).
\]
Let $q\in X_\alpha$. Since $q\notin\operatorname{Sing}(\mathcal F)$ and, by the standing
condition, both hypersurfaces are smooth at $q$, choose a holomorphic
flow box
\(
(z,t)\in\Delta\times\Delta
\)
in which
\(
\mathcal F=\{t=\text{constant}\}.
\)
Since $M_0$ and $M_\alpha$ are invariant, after shrinking the box they
have the form
\[
M_0=\{t\in\gamma_0\},\qquad
M_\alpha=\{t\in\gamma_\alpha\},
\]
where $\gamma_0$ and $\gamma_\alpha$ are smooth real-analytic curve
germs in the transverse disc.

The two transverse curve germs cannot coincide. Indeed, equality of
the transverse germs would imply equality of the two saturated
hypersurface germs in the flow box; since $M_0$ and $M_\alpha$ are
 irreducible real-analytic variety of pure real codimension one, analytic continuation would
then give $M_0=M_\alpha$, contrary to the hypothesis. Hence
$\gamma_0\cap\gamma_\alpha$ is discrete. It follows that $X_\alpha$ is
locally a union of plaques $\{t=t_j\}$ and therefore is a
one-dimensional complex analytic subset of
\(
\mathbb P^2\setminus\operatorname{Sing}(\mathcal F).
\)
Every irreducible component is invariant by $\mathcal F$.

The singular set of a foliation on $\mathbb P^2$ is finite. Since
$M_0\cap M_\alpha$ is closed in $\mathbb P^2$, an irreducible component of
$X_\alpha$ can acquire boundary, in passing to $\mathbb P^2$, only at points
of $\operatorname{Sing}(\mathcal F)$. The Remmert--Stein extension theorem therefore shows
that its closure is a one-dimensional complex analytic subset of
$\mathbb P^2$. By Chow's theorem this closure is algebraic. Thus, for every
relevant $\alpha$, choose an irreducible invariant algebraic curve
\[
C_\alpha\subset M_0\cap M_\alpha.
\]

If infinitely many distinct curves $C_\alpha$ occur, then $\mathcal F$ has
infinitely many invariant algebraic curves. By the Darboux--Jouanolou
theorem \cite{Jouanolou}, $\mathcal F$ admits a nonconstant rational first
integral; this is alternative \textup{(i)}.

Assume instead that only finitely many distinct curves $C_\alpha$
occur. By the pigeonhole principle, one of them, say $C$, is contained
in infinitely many members $M_{\alpha_j}$ of the family. Let $L$ be a
connected regular leaf component of
\[
C\setminus\operatorname{Sing}(\mathcal F),
\]
and choose a small complex transversal $(\Sigma,q)\simeq(\mathbb C,0)$ to
$L$. Each $M_{\alpha_j}$ determines a smooth real-analytic transverse
curve germ
\[
\gamma_j=M_{\alpha_j}\cap\Sigma.
\]
Because $M_{\alpha_j}$ is saturated by $\mathcal F$, every element of the
virtual holonomy group of $L$ preserves $\gamma_j$. Moreover these
transverse germs are pairwise distinct: equality of two of them would
imply equality of the corresponding saturated hypersurface germs, and
irreducibility and real-analytic continuation would then imply equality
of the global Levi-flats. Proposition~\ref{prop:many-leviflats-holonomy}
therefore gives that the virtual holonomy group of $L$ is abelian.
This proves alternative \textup{(ii)} and the virtual-holonomy
assertion.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Assume now the additional hypotheses in the last paragraph of
Theorem~\ref{thm:leviflat-intersection-alternative}. On every connected
component $L$ of $C\setminus\operatorname{Sing}(\mathcal F)$, the virtual holonomy group is
abelian. By Lemma~\ref{lem:abelian-invariant-form}, on a transverse disc
there is a nonzero invariant formal meromorphic differential. Suspending
it along $L$ gives a closed formal meromorphic $1$-form
\[
\widehat\eta_L
\]
on the formal neighborhood of $L$, defining $\mathcal F$ there. Holonomy
invariance is precisely the condition making the suspension
single-valued.

Let
\[
\pi:S=\operatorname{Bl}_{p_1,\ldots,p_m}\mathbb P^2\longrightarrow\mathbb P^2
\]
be the blow-up of the dicritical singularities occurring in the theorem,
and let $\widetilde C$ be the strict transform of $C$. Pull back the
formal form to the regular part of $\widetilde C$. By hypothesis, every
singularity of the transformed foliation on $\widetilde C$ lying over a
dicritical point is reduced, non-dicritical, and is not a saddle-node;
the other singularities were already reduced and non-saddle-node. Since $C$ is
contained in infinitely many invariant real-analytic Levi-flat germs,
the same is true after pull-back along $\widetilde C$. The local theorem
of Cerveau--Lins Neto \cite{CLN}, or Brunella's formulation
\cite{Brunella}, supplies a nonconstant local meromorphic first integral
at these singular points. In the reduced non-dicritical non-saddle-node
case this is the analytically linearizable resonant situation; hence in
suitable local coordinates one has a primitive first integral
\[
H=x^n y^m,\qquad n,m\ge1,
\]
and a closed logarithmic defining form
\[
\eta_0=\frac{dH}{H}
=n\frac{dx}{x}+m\frac{dy}{y}.
\]
On the punctured formal neighborhood of the branch of $\widetilde C$
approaching such a point,
\[
\widehat\eta_L=\Phi\,\eta_0.
\]
Closedness gives $d\Phi\wedge\eta_0=0$, so $\Phi$ is a formal
meromorphic first integral and therefore $\Phi=\varphi(H)$ for a
one-variable formal meromorphic germ $\varphi$. Since $H=x^ny^m$
vanishes on the invariant axes, $\varphi(H)$ is formal meromorphic at
the origin. Thus the form extends formally meromorphically through the
point.

We must also check compatibility when two invariant components meet at
a corner. Let $q$ be such a point and let $\widehat\eta_1$ and
$\widehat\eta_2$ be the closed formal meromorphic forms obtained from
the two sides. Since they define the same foliation, on their common
formal domain one has
\[
\widehat\eta_1=\Psi\,\widehat\eta_2,
\]
where closedness implies
\[
d\Psi\wedge\widehat\eta_2=0.
\]
Hence $\Psi$ is a formal meromorphic first integral. If the germ has no
nonconstant meromorphic first integral, then $\Psi$ is constant and the
two forms glue after a constant normalization. The only remaining
possibility at a reduced non-dicritical corner is the resonant
integrable case, analytically conjugate to
\[
d(x^n y^m)=0.
\]
There the finite-to-finite Dulac correspondence identifies the
transverse dynamics of the two components. Equivalently, one adjoins the
holonomy groups of the adjacent components through the Dulac
correspondence. By construction, this adjoined holonomy group is still
contained in the virtual holonomy group of the leaf under consideration.
Since the latter is abelian in our situation, the adjoined group is
abelian as well. Hence the invariant transverse formal differential is
the same on both sides, up to the same constant normalization, and the
suspended closed forms are compatible. This is the standard adjunction
mechanism for holonomy groups along a reducible invariant divisor; see
Camacho--Lins Neto--Sad~\cite{CamachoLinsNetoSad},
Paul~\cite{Paul1999}, Camacho--Sc\'ardua~\cite{CamachoScarduaLiouvillian},
and Sc\'ardua~\cite{ScarduaBoundedGeometry}.

Consequently the local extensions agree through all corners and all
singular points of $\widetilde C$. Performing this at all points of
$\widetilde C$ gives a global closed formal meromorphic $1$-form
\[
\widehat\eta
\]
on the formal completion $\widehat S_{\widetilde C}$, defining the
transformed foliation formally along $\widetilde C$.

We now use the numerical hypothesis. Write
\[
d=\deg C,\qquad d_j=\operatorname{mult}_{p_j}(C).
\]
On the blown-up surface,
\[
\widetilde C^{\,2}=d^2-\sum_{j=1}^m d_j^2.
\]
Since
\(
\sum_{j=1}^m d_j<d,
\)
we have
\[
\sum_{j=1}^m d_j^2
\le \left(\sum_{j=1}^m d_j\right)^2<d^2,
\]
and therefore
\(
\widetilde C^{\,2}>0.
\)
This is the numerical condition used by Sad in his treatment of
controlled dicritical singularities; radial singularities are among the
allowed examples \cite{Sad1995}.

Hironaka--Matsumura, Proposition~3.6 in \cite{HM}, states that if $D$ is
an effective divisor on a nonsingular projective surface, $D^2>0$, and
every prime component of $D$ has nonnegative self-intersection, then the
field of formal-rational functions along $\operatorname{Supp}(D)$ equals
the rational function field of the surface. Applying this to the
irreducible divisor $D=\widetilde C$ gives
\[
K\!\left(\widehat S_{\widetilde C}\right)=K(S).
\]
Choose rational coordinates $(u,v)$ on a dense affine chart of $S$ and
write
\[
\widehat\eta=\widehat A\,du+\widehat B\,dv.
\]
The coefficients belong to
$K(\widehat S_{\widetilde C})=K(S)$, hence they are the formal germs of
rational functions $A,B\in K(S)$. Therefore
\[
\eta_S=A\,du+B\,dv
\]
is a rational $1$-form on $S$ whose formal completion along
$\widetilde C$ is $\widehat\eta$. Injectivity of the completion map
shows that
\[
d\eta_S=0
\]
and, if $\omega_S$ is a rational defining form of the transformed
foliation, that
\[
\eta_S\wedge\omega_S=0.
\]
Thus $\eta_S$ is a closed rational defining form for the transformed
foliation.

Finally, $\pi$ is birational, so
\[
K(S)=K(\mathbb P^2)
\]
and hence
\[
\Omega^1_{K(S)/\mathbb C}=\Omega^1_{K(\mathbb P^2)/\mathbb C}.
\]
Thus $\eta_S$ is the pull-back, in the rational category, of a unique
rational $1$-form $\eta$ on $\mathbb P^2$. The identities above descend to
\[
d\eta=0,
\qquad
\eta\wedge\omega_{\mathcal F}=0,
\]
for any rational defining form $\omega_{\mathcal F}$ of $\mathcal F$. Consequently
$\eta$ is a nonzero closed rational $1$-form defining $\mathcal F$.
head: environment

label: rem:H-branch
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{rem:H-branch}
Hypothesis \textup{(H)} isolates the branch in which one Levi-flat meets
infinitely many others at regular points of the foliation. It is not
automatic. For a rational pencil one may choose infinitely many
pairwise disjoint real-analytic curves in the parameter sphere; their
inverse images are invariant Levi-flats which may meet only at the base
locus. The next result addresses a model for this separated branch.
head: environment

label: thm:separated-leviflats-closed-form
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:separated-leviflats-closed-form}
Let $\mathcal F$ be a holomorphic foliation on $\mathbb P^2$, let
\[
p\in\operatorname{Sing}(\mathcal F),
\]
and let
\[
F_p:(U,p)\dashrightarrow\mathbb P^1
\]
be a minimal local meromorphic first integral. Assume that $\mathcal F$ admits infinitely many pairwise distinct irreducible
global invariant real-analytic Levi-flat varieties $M_j$ passing through
$p$ and such that
\[
(M_j\cap M_k)\cap(U\setminus\{p\})=\varnothing,
\qquad j\neq k.
\]
Assume finally that the minimal transverse parameter admits projectively
compatible analytic continuation throughout $\mathbb P^2\setminus\operatorname{Sing}(\mathcal F)$,
in the sense that the changes of minimal parameter are M\"obius
transformations and that, for each $M_j$, one connected component of the
local transverse trace associated with a branch of $M_j$ at $p$ continues
to a compact real-analytic subset $\gamma_j\subset\mathbb P^1$ of pure real
dimension one. Assume moreover that the continued sets $\gamma_j$ are
pairwise disjoint and that each of them is preserved individually by the
projective monodromy. Then $\mathcal F$ is defined on $\mathbb P^2$ by a nonzero
closed rational $1$-form.
head: environment
name: Separated pencil-type Levi-flats

label: lem:mobius-separated-curves
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:mobius-separated-curves}
Let
\[
G\subset\operatorname{PGL}(2,\mathbb C)
\]
be a group of M\"obius transformations. Assume that there exists an
infinite family
\[
\{\gamma_j\}_{j\in J}
\]
of pairwise disjoint, connected, compact real-analytic subsets of
$\mathbb P^1$, each of pure real dimension one, such that
\[
g(\gamma_j)=\gamma_j
\]
for every $g\in G$ and every $j\in J$. Then there exists a nonzero
rational $1$-form $\theta$ on $\mathbb P^1$ such that
\[
g^*\theta=\theta
\qquad\text{for every }g\in G.
\]
In particular, $\theta$ is closed.
head: environment
name: Transverse M\"obius-group lemma

title: Proof
body_md:
Choose three distinct members
\[
\gamma_1,\gamma_2,\gamma_3
\]
and points $z_j\in\gamma_j$. Since the sets $\gamma_j$ are compact and
pairwise disjoint, their mutual spherical distances are positive.

Let $(g_\nu)$ be any sequence in $G$. Since
\[
g_\nu(z_j)\in\gamma_j,
\qquad j=1,2,3,
\]
after passing to a subsequence we may assume that
\[
g_\nu(z_j)\longrightarrow w_j\in\gamma_j,
\qquad j=1,2,3.
\]
The points $w_1,w_2,w_3$ are pairwise distinct. Since a M\"obius
transformation is uniquely determined by the images of three distinct
points, the sequence $(g_\nu)$ has a convergent subsequence in
$\operatorname{PGL}(2,\mathbb C)$. Hence
\[
K=\overline G
\]
is a compact subgroup of $\operatorname{PGL}(2,\mathbb C)$. Passing to the
limit in $g(\gamma_j)=\gamma_j$, we also have
\[
k(\gamma_j)=\gamma_j
\qquad\text{for every }k\in K\text{ and every }j.
\]

If $K$ is finite, let
\[
q:\mathbb P^1\longrightarrow\mathbb P^1/K
\]
be the quotient map. Since $\mathbb P^1/K\simeq\mathbb P^1$, choose a nonzero
rational $1$-form $\beta$ on the quotient and put
\[
\theta=q^*\beta.
\]
Then $\theta$ is a nonzero rational $K$-invariant $1$-form, hence it is
$G$-invariant.

Assume now that $K$ is infinite. Every compact subgroup of
$\operatorname{PGL}(2,\mathbb C)$ is M\"obius-conjugate to a subgroup of
$\operatorname{PSU}(2)$. Since $K$ preserves the proper one-dimensional
sets $\gamma_j$, it cannot be all of $\operatorname{PSU}(2)$. Hence its
identity component $K^0$ is a circle subgroup. After a M\"obius change
of coordinate we may assume that
\[
K^0=\{z\mapsto e^{it}z;\ t\in\mathbb R\}.
\]

Each $\gamma_j$ is connected, $K^0$-invariant, and of pure real
dimension one. The nontrivial $K^0$-orbits are the circles
\(
|z|=r.
\)
If some $\gamma_j$ contained orbits with more than one value of $r$, it
would contain a real two-dimensional annular subset, contrary to its
pure real dimension one. Thus
\(
\gamma_j=\{|z|=r_j\}
\)
for some $r_j>0$.

It remains to show that $K$ itself is contained in this circle group.
An element of the normalizer of $K^0$ which is not in $K^0$ interchanges
the fixed points $0$ and $\infty$ and has the form
\[
z\longmapsto\frac{a}{z}.
\]
Such a map sends
\[
\{|z|=r\}
\quad\text{to}\quad
\{|z|=|a|/r\}.
\]
It can therefore preserve individually at most one circle of the
family, namely the circle satisfying $r^2=|a|$. Since the family
$\{\gamma_j\}$ is infinite and every member is preserved individually
by every element of $K$, no such element can belong to $K$. Therefore
\[
K\subset\{z\mapsto e^{it}z\}.
\]
Consequently
\[
\theta=\frac{dz}{z}
\]
is invariant under $K$, and hence under $G$. Pulling $\theta$ back by
the initial M\"obius conjugacy gives the required nonzero rational
$G$-invariant $1$-form on $\mathbb P^1$. Since every meromorphic $1$-form on
a Riemann surface is closed, the proof is complete.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let
\[
G\subset\operatorname{PGL}(2,\mathbb C)
\]
be the projective monodromy group of the analytically continued minimal
transverse parameter. For each $j$, choose the connected component of the local transverse
trace specified in the continuation hypothesis and denote its continued
image by
\[
\gamma_j\subset\mathbb P^1.
\]
By assumption, the sets $\gamma_j$ are connected, compact, pairwise
disjoint real-analytic subsets of pure real dimension one, and each of them
is preserved by every element of $G$.

By Lemma~\ref{lem:mobius-separated-curves}, there exists a nonzero
rational $1$-form $\theta$ on $\mathbb P^1$ such that
\[
A^*\theta=\theta
\qquad\text{for every }A\in G.
\]
Choose local branches $F_\alpha$ of the analytically continued minimal
parameter and define
\(
\eta_\alpha=F_\alpha^*\theta.
\)
If
\(
F_\beta=A_{\beta\alpha}\circ F_\alpha,
\qquad A_{\beta\alpha}\in G,
\)
then
\(
\eta_\beta
 =F_\alpha^*(A_{\beta\alpha}^*\theta)
 =F_\alpha^*\theta
 =\eta_\alpha.
\)
Thus the local forms glue on $\mathbb P^2\setminus\operatorname{Sing}(\mathcal F)$ to a
single meromorphic $1$-form $\eta$ defining $\mathcal F$ there. Since
$\operatorname{Sing}(\mathcal F)$ is finite, $\eta$ extends meromorphically across it.
On the projective surface $\mathbb P^2$, every meromorphic $1$-form is
rational. Moreover $d\theta=0$ on the parameter sphere, hence
$d\eta=0$. Therefore $\mathcal F$ is defined by a nonzero closed rational
$1$-form.
head: environment

label: cor:separated-one-dicritical
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{cor:separated-one-dicritical}
In Theorem~\ref{thm:separated-leviflats-closed-form}, suppose that $p$
is the only dicritical singularity involved in the separated family.
Then no compatibility condition between different dicritical points is
needed: it is enough that one minimal local parameter at $p$ continue
projectively throughout $\mathbb P^2\setminus\operatorname{Sing}(\mathcal F)$ and that the associated
connected transverse parameter sets satisfy the separation and individual
invariance hypotheses of Theorem~\ref{thm:separated-leviflats-closed-form}.
The conclusion is again that $\mathcal F$ is defined by a nonzero closed rational
$1$-form.
head: environment
name: One relevant dicritical point

label: thm:stein
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:stein}
Let $X$ be a Stein manifold of complex dimension $n\ge3$, let $\mathcal F$ be
a codimension-one holomorphic foliation on $X$, and let $M\subset X$
be a connected irreducible real-analytic variety of pure real codimension one 
invariant by $\mathcal F$. Assume:

\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)}]
\item
\[
\operatorname{Sing}(M)\subset\operatorname{Sing}(\mathcal F);
\]

\item all dicritical singularities of $\mathcal F$ contained in $M$ belong to
an irreducible codimension-two analytic subset
\[
D\subset M\cap\operatorname{Sing}(\mathcal F),
\]
and $D$ is generically of local product type;

\item there exists a pencil singularity for $M$ in the local-product
locus of $D$;

\item the generic transverse parameter along $D^\circ$ has no
transverse degree jump along $D$ in the sense of
Definition~\ref{def:no-degree-jump}.
\end{enumerate}

Then there exist an open neighborhood $N\supset M$ and a nonconstant
meromorphic first integral
\[
G\in\mathcal M(N)
\]
of $\mathcal F|_N$.

If, in addition, there exists a compact set $K\subset X$ such that
\[
X\setminus K\subset N
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
X\setminus K\ \text{is connected},
\]
then $G$ extends meromorphically to $X$, and $\mathcal F$ admits a nonconstant
global meromorphic first integral on $X$.
head: environment
name: Stein-manifold version

title: Proof
body_md:
The semi-global argument used in the proof of Theorem~\ref{thm:semiglobal} gives a
nonconstant meromorphic first integral
\[
G\in\mathcal M(N)
\]
on a neighborhood $N\supset M$.

Assume now that there is a compact set $K\subset X$ such that
\[
X\setminus K\subset N
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
X\setminus K\ \text{is connected}.
\]
The restriction of $G$ to $X\setminus K$ extends meromorphically
through $K$ by the meromorphic Hartogs extension theorem on the Stein
manifold $X$. We obtain
\[
\widetilde G\in\mathcal M(X).
\]
By uniqueness of meromorphic continuation, $\widetilde G$ agrees with
$G$ wherever both are defined. Since
\[
dG\wedge\omega=0
\]
near $M$, analytic continuation gives
\[
d\widetilde G\wedge\omega=0
\]
wherever $\omega$ defines $\mathcal F$. Thus $\widetilde G$ is a nonconstant
global meromorphic first integral of $\mathcal F$.

label: cor:higher-dimensional-dicritical
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{cor:higher-dimensional-dicritical}
Let $\mathcal F$ be a codimension-one holomorphic foliation on $\mathbb P^n$,
$n\ge3$, and let
\[
M\subset\mathbb P^n
\]
be an irreducible real-analytic variety of pure real codimension one  invariant by
$\mathcal F$. Assume that
\[
\operatorname{Sing}(M)\subset\operatorname{Sing}(\mathcal F)
\]
and that every singularity of $\mathcal F$ contained in $M$ is dicritical.

Choose a finite collection of neighborhoods
\(
U_1,\ldots,U_r
\)
covering $\operatorname{Sing}(\mathcal F)\cap M$, and, after shrinking if necessary, choose
on each $U_j$ a minimal meromorphic first integral
\(
H_j:U_j\dashrightarrow\mathbb P^1
\)
for $\mathcal F|_{U_j}$.

Assume that whenever a generic global Levi leaf
$L\subset M_{\mathrm{reg}}$ enters a sufficiently small neighborhood of
$\operatorname{Sing}(\mathcal F)\cap M$ contained in $U_j$, all the corresponding local
branches of $L$ determine the same value
\[
\lambda_j(L)\in\mathbb P^1
\]
of $H_j$. Assume moreover that the local parameters are projectively
compatible: there exist transformations
\[
A_{ji}\in\operatorname{PGL}(2,\mathbb C)
\]
depending only on the pair $(i,j)$, and not on the Levi leaf, such that
whenever a generic global Levi leaf $L$ is represented in both
$U_i$ and $U_j$ one has
\[
\lambda_j(L)=A_{ji}\bigl(\lambda_i(L)\bigr),
\]
and the maps $A_{ji}$ satisfy
\[
A_{ii}=\operatorname{id},
\qquad
A_{kj}\circ A_{ji}=A_{ki}
\]
whenever all terms are defined.

Then $\mathcal F$ admits a nonconstant rational first integral on $\mathbb P^n$.
head: environment
name: All singularities on $M$ dicritical

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $L\subset M_{\mathrm{reg}}$ be a Levi leaf. Its closure
\(
\overline L\subset M\subset\mathbb P^n
\)
is a nonempty compact $\mathcal F$-invariant set. By a theorem of
Lins Neto on nontrivial minimal sets in projective space
\cite{LinsNeto1999}, a codimension-one holomorphic foliation on
$\mathbb P^n$, $n\ge3$, has no nontrivial minimal set. Consequently
$\overline L$ meets $\operatorname{Sing}(\mathcal F)$. Since every singularity of $\mathcal F$
contained in $M$ is dicritical, every Levi leaf accumulates on the
dicritical locus in $M$.

The finite family $U_1,\ldots,U_r$ therefore meets the accumulation
set of every Levi leaf. The constancy assumption allows the local
parameters $H_j$ to be transported along the Levi foliation, and the
M\"obius compatibility and cocycle relations identify the resulting
parameters on overlaps. Thus the same holonomy argument as in
Proposition~\ref{prop:nearMreg} produces a single-valued meromorphic
first integral on a neighborhood of $M_{\mathrm{reg}}$.

Each $H_j$ supplies the extension through the singular set covered by
$U_1,\ldots,U_r$. Hence the first integral is meromorphic on a
neighborhood $N$ of all of $M$. For each connected component $\Omega$
of $\mathbb P^n\setminus M$, Proposition~\ref{prop:pseudoconvex} and
Takeuchi's theorem imply that $\Omega$ is Stein. Applying
Lemma~\ref{lem:boundary-hartogs} to $G|_{N\cap\Omega}$ and shrinking $N$
near $M$ if necessary extends the first integral through every
complementary component. The resulting global meromorphic function on
$\mathbb P^n$ is necessarily rational.
